title: S&P upgrades Sri Lanka, says out of default danger zone | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 28 November 2026 00:00
-     - 25

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake

S&P Global Ratings yesterday upgraded Sri Lanka’s long-term sovereign credit ratings to ‘B-’ from ‘CCC+’, with a stable outlook, saying the country’s willingness and capacity to repay its debt obligations had become less vulnerable to unfavourable external financing conditions, and that a default over the next two years was unlikely.

S&P also raised its short-term foreign and local currency ratings to ‘B’ from ‘C’. The transfer and convertibility assessment is unchanged at ‘B-’.

The rating agency said the stable outlook reflects its expectations that Sri Lanka’s economy will remain resilient over the next six to 12 months, despite prolonged disruptions to the global energy market, while the Government continues to build fiscal and external buffers through policies that improve macroeconomic stability.

“The ‘B-’ ratings reflect our assessment that the improvements in Sri Lanka’s macroeconomic settings have become more entrenched. This has led to a steady increase in fiscal and external buffers, which supports the Government’s capacity to manage further external volatility and the heavier external debt repayments in the coming years. We believe Sri Lanka’s willingness and capacity to repay debt obligations is less vulnerable to unfavourable external financing conditions, and that a default scenario over the next two years is unlikely,” it added.

However, the rating agency said risks remain high, as Sri Lanka is vulnerable to global shortages of crude oil and petrochemicals. The prolonged war in the Middle East will maintain pressure on the external balance, particularly if remittances falter. The impending El Nino could affect hydropower generation and agricultural production, worsening inflationary concerns and dampening growth.

It noted that despite substantial improvements in recent years, the general Government interest burden, at about 40% of revenue, is still heavy.

S&P believes support from multilateral institutions is likely to continue, and that the country’s economic recovery and structural reform efforts to anchor further fiscal and external improvements should remain intact.

“We expect Sri Lanka’s economic growth to slow to 4% in 2026 and rebound to 4.5% in 2027. We forecast Sri Lanka’s 10-year weighted average per capita real GDP growth at 3.2%. This is in line with peers with similar income levels and indicates that Sri Lanka has largely shaken off the effects of its 2022 economic crisis. We believe Sri Lanka’s GDP per capita would reach $ 5,200 in 2026 despite a weakening Sri Lankan rupee,” it added.

The agency said Sri Lanka’s economy has fared well so far despite the abrupt outbreak of the Middle East war. Proactive policy responses, including rationing fuel and shortening the work week, helped to preserve supply early and reduce disruptions to industrial and agricultural activities. Although real GDP growth slowed to 4.2% year-on-year (YoY) in the second quarter of 2026 from 5.1% in the first quarter, manufacturing industrial production expanded for nine months this year through to September.

S&P said it anticipates the Government will continue the reform agenda under the current International Monetary Fund (IMF) Extended Fund Facility program even after the program ends in March 2027, including implementing revenue-based Budget repair, cost-recovery pricing for utilities and other structural reforms of public financial and debt management. It added that the Government has demonstrated strong commitment to the IMF program, meeting most of the quantitative indicators and structural benchmarks, albeit some with delays, even under challenging circumstances.

On the fiscal front, the agency noted that Sri Lanka’s fiscal position has improved significantly since 2022, underpinned by a series of revenue measures and robust economic growth. The revenue growth momentum has not faltered much this year despite the more challenging external environment and moderation in economic growth. Government revenue grew 20% YoY in the first nine months of 2026, despite the strong base in 2025.

“We expect general Government revenue to exceed 17% of GDP in 2026, roughly double the rate in 2022. Even if growth slows substantially in the last quarter and expenditure execution improves, we expect the overall fiscal deficit to narrow in 2026 to below 2% of GDP. The primary balance will likely remain in surplus for four consecutive years,” it added.

On the expenditure front, the rating agency noted that spending is higher this year due to larger subsidies and transfers, as the Government disbursed, albeit slowly, funds for post-disaster relief and reconstruction for Cyclone Ditwah, which occurred in November 2025.

It said capital expenditure has also accelerated YoY in the first three quarters of this year, and it expects a further ramp-up in the last quarter. As a result, the agency projects that the fiscal deficit will increase to 1.8% of GDP in 2026, despite the Government running a surplus in the first nine months.

“We expect the fiscal deficit to widen in 2027 due to the various support measures introduced in the Budget, including the increase in the personal income tax thresholds, removal of the Value-Added Tax (VAT) on school supplies, and reductions in targeted levies, such as for solar batteries,” it added.

The agency expects Sri Lanka’s current account to flip to a deficit of 1.4% of GDP in 2026, while gross external financing needs as a share of current account receipts and usable reserves will widen to about 109% this year, from 104% in 2025, before improving to 104% by 2029. This still compares favourably with the pre-crisis average of more than 120%. It expects external debt net of public and financial sector external assets to average 96% of current account receipts over 2026-2029.

It also noted that gross official reserves fell to $ 6.5 billion in June before recovering to $ 7.09 billion in October. Remittances were still rising as of September 2026, but at a slower pace, while tourism earnings declined by 9.2% in the first nine months.

S&P forecasts net general Government debt, including State-owned enterprise (SOE) guarantees, at about 92% of GDP for 2026.

The rating agency said it could raise Sri Lanka’s ratings if two or more of the following become likely: the interest burden as a share of revenue falls substantially to levels more consistent with most countries it rates; net external debt falls below current account receipts on a sustained basis; the change in net general Government debt is consistently about 3% of GDP; and macroeconomic stability becomes more entrenched, with financing conditions normalising to the extent that the Government’s willingness to default reduces substantially.

Conversely, it said it could lower the ratings if it sees indications of renewed risks of funding and liquidity stresses, which could be preceded by significantly weaker external or fiscal performance.

The Colombo Port’s East Terminal (ECT) is expected to begin operations at 50% capacity by the end of this month, following the completion of its automated yard operations, Ports and Civil Aviation Deputy Minister Janitha Ruwan Kodithuwakku said yesterday.

Speaking during an inspection of operational activities at the terminal, Kodithuwakku said the Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) had faced several challenges in completing the terminal’s semi-automated yard, but the work had since been completed through the intervention of its officials and engineers.

“One lane commenced today, and we expect to commence the remaining 10 lanes within this month,” he said.

The automated yard now operates with Automated Rail Mounted Gantry (ARMG) cranes, and the terminal is expected to achieve an operational efficiency of 20 to 30 containers per hour, he added.

The East Terminal, which consists of a quay wall and a yard equipped with gantry cranes, has faced delays over the years due to various challenges, Kodithuwakku said.

The terminal is capable of handling some of the world’s largest vessels and will facilitate the handling of import containers as well as containers transshipped through other terminals. Its automated yard operations can be carried out with approximately 100 employees and are designed to comply with international security standards.

Several senior SLPA officials were also present during the inspection.

Designed for audiences across generations, it will give families, friends and international visitors a place to celebrate Christmas together.

The project draws on years of experience in conceptualising and designing Christmas installations across Colombo. It consolidates that work into a single destination, built to return every year and to attract both domestic and international visitors.

Beyond entertainment, Colombo Christmas is intended to give travellers a compelling reason to include Colombo in their December plans. title: Sri Lanka leads global study in AI-assisted shopping, new research reveals | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 28 November 2026 00:00
-     - 19

Sri Lankan consumers are leading the way in Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered shopping, according to new international research from digital product consultancy Apadmi.

The ‘Mobile Loyalty Report 2026: Global Edition,’ which surveyed 3,300 consumers across 11 markets, reveals that 71% of Sri Lankans use AI assistants at least weekly when making purchasing decisions, compared with 45% across all surveyed markets, 43% in the US, and 41% in the UK.

Sri Lanka also leads on daily adoption, with 29% using AI assistants every day to help them shop, more than double the 13% average.

The research covers AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Gemini, as well as AI features built into retailers’ own apps and websites.

Sri Lankan shoppers embrace AI, but want to stay in control

The findings reveal a strong appetite for practical AI assistance, particularly when it helps consumers find better value.

More than half of Sri Lankan respondents (56%) would allow AI to compare prices and find the best deal, compared with 43% across the surveyed markets. Meanwhile, 27% would let AI apply offers and loyalty points automatically. 

However, just 6% would allow AI to complete a purchase without checking first. Only 5% would reject every AI-assisted shopping task surveyed, compared with 23% across all markets.

The findings suggest that Sri Lankan consumers are ready to embrace AI as a shopping adviser, but still want control over final purchasing decisions.

Deals and convenience matter more than loyalty points

Sri Lanka also stands apart in how consumers use loyalty apps. Just 13% keep a brand’s app mainly to collect loyalty points, compared with 40% across the 11 markets.

Instead, Sri Lankan shoppers are more interested in practical benefits. Some 34% keep apps because they make products easier to find and buy, while 33% value access to the latest offers.

The research also found that 40% of Sri Lankan consumers wait for member offers before making a purchase, the highest proportion across the 11 markets and significantly above the 29% average.

This presents a challenge for retailers relying on traditional points-based loyalty schemes. For Sri Lankan consumers, immediate value, relevant offers, and convenience are important reasons to keep an app.

Loyalty is valuable, but not unconditional

The research also reveals how loyalty apps influence purchasing decisions. Some 43% of Sri Lankan shoppers say loyalty apps encourage them to shop with a brand more often, while 21% say they buy items through a loyalty app that they would otherwise have purchased from a competitor.

More than a quarter (26%) say they remain loyal to a brand even when a rival offers a cheaper price, the highest proportion recorded across the 11 markets. However, 23% say their loyalty app makes no difference to how they shop.

For retailers, the findings highlight the importance of delivering meaningful value rather than relying on membership alone to secure repeat purchases.

What this means for Sri Lankan retailers

The findings point towards a new generation of mobile loyalty experiences that combine practical AI assistance, relevant offers, and easy-to-use shopping features.

With Sri Lankan consumers already comfortable using AI to inform their purchases, retailers have an opportunity to bring price comparisons, personalised recommendations, and relevant offers directly into their existing apps.

But the research also suggests that technology alone is not enough. Consumers want experiences that make shopping easier, provide clear value, and leave them in control.

Apadmi Growth Director Naadira Jumat said: “For retailers, the message is clear: loyalty isn’t just about collecting points anymore. It’s about making every shopping experience easier, more useful, and better value. We’ve seen first-hand through our work with Keells how important mobile loyalty experiences are becoming for consumers. The opportunity now is for brands to build on that foundation, bringing AI-powered recommendations and relevant offers into apps customers already use and trust.”

Apadmi’s ‘Mobile Loyalty Report 2026: Global Edition’ explores consumer attitudes towards loyalty programs, mobile apps, data sharing, and AI-assisted shopping across 11 international markets, including Sri Lanka. To download the full report, visit: https://www.apadmi.com/download/mobile-loyalty-report-2026-global-edition/

The ‘Mobile Loyalty Report 2026: Global Edition’ is based on a survey of over 3,300 consumers across 11 markets, using nationally representative samples. References to AI assistants include ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, and Alexa, alongside AI functionality built into retailers’ own apps and websites. The findings relate to the use of AI in making purchasing decisions, not necessarily completing purchases. The Sri Lankan 55+ sample is excluded from age-group comparisons due to insufficient sample size.

title: Sri Lanka has 1-2 year window to woo Indian manufacturing investment, warns CCC | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 28 November 2026 00:00
-     - 21

Ceylon Chamber CEO Shiran Fernando

- Pic by Lasantha Kumara

By Charumini de Silva

The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce (CCC) CEO Shiran Fernando has warned that Sri Lanka has a narrow one-to-two-year window to position itself as an alternative manufacturing destination for Indian businesses, but high operating costs and delays in domestic reforms could undermine its ability to capture the emerging investment opportunity.

Speaking at a panel discussion organised by the Asian Development Bank (ADB) Serendipity Knowledge Program’s Trade Reform Forum, he said Indian business interest in Sri Lanka had increased considerably, with the Chamber facilitating around 15 business delegations since April 2026, of which an estimated 50%-60% had come from India.

“The engagement extended beyond major national business organisations to regional industry associations and State-level business groups,” he said, pointing to growing interest in Sri Lanka as a destination for investment, manufacturing and regional partnerships.

Citing an example, Fernando said an Indian footwear manufacturer from Chennai, which exports to the EU and US markets, had visited Sri Lanka to explore relocating part of its manufacturing operations.

“Although the company had expressed interest in Sri Lanka, its key concern was the country’s cost competitiveness, with the overall cost of production estimated to be 25%-30% higher after accounting for labour, financing and other operating expenses,” he added.

Fernando said this highlighted the urgency of accelerating reforms in labour regulations, electricity costs and other business-related expenses to make Sri Lanka a more attractive manufacturing destination.

“There is a real opportunity for these $ 2-3 million investments to come in and scale at a much bigger pace,” he said, warning that Sri Lanka had perhaps a couple of years to convince prospective investors and convert the growing interest into actual investments.

He also stressed that India’s importance to Sri Lanka extended beyond bilateral trade, with opportunities emerging through third-country businesses seeking to access South Asian markets through the island.

“Business delegations and investment agencies from countries including the US and other Western nations were engaging with their counterparts in India to explore opportunities in Sri Lanka,” he said.

Fernando cited visits by foreign investment promotion agencies and business representatives based in New Delhi and other Indian cities as evidence of this emerging trend.

title: Search for Sri Lanka’s ‘Coolest Projects’ is on, with ComBank empowering young tech talent | Daily FT
summary:

Some of the contestants from last year’s Coolest Projects competition

The search for Sri Lanka’s ‘Coolest Projects’ is in full swing, with Commercial Bank of Ceylon PLC once again reaffirming, its strategic commitment to uplifting national education. 

Having established over 450 IT Labs and 200 STEM classrooms island-wide to build the technical capabilities of school children, the Bank is championing this nationwide initiative as the definitive platform for youth to showcase their digital proficiency. As registrations draw to a close, the next stage of mentoring and innovation beckons. 

Powered by Commercial Bank in partnership with the STEMUp Educational Foundation, the official local partner of the UK-based Raspberry Pi Foundation, Coolest Projects Sri Lanka 2026 is inviting young creators under 18 years of age to demonstrate how imagination, curiosity and technology can “achieve greater things.” The competition offers participants the opportunity to showcase their digital projects, receive one-to-one guidance from industry professionals and gain exposure on a platform built around international standards of innovation. 

With submissions accepted from individuals and teams of up to three members, the competition aims to attract 500 applications from school students across all provinces, opening the door to a diverse range of ideas, experiences and approaches to solving real-world problems through technology.

The focus will soon shift from submissions to selection, as an independent evaluation panel prepares to identify the 100 best-performing entries for the next stage, the Bank said. Entries will be assessed on their creativity, complexity, presentation and usability, before the selected entrants embark on a structured mentoring journey to refine their software and hardware prototypes ahead of the national showcase and awards ceremony, tentatively scheduled for December at Trace Expert City, Colombo.

The possibilities are as varied as the young minds behind the projects. Categories include hardware, Scratch programming, web development, advanced programming and app development, creating space for students with different interests and levels of technical experience to explore their potential. The emphasis is not simply on what participants can build, but on how effectively they can apply technology, solve problems and communicate their ideas.

A defining feature of Coolest Projects is its commitment to making opportunity accessible beyond the country’s main urban centres. More than 60% of participants have come from rural schools outside Colombo, highlighting the potential of the initiative to connect young people with opportunities for learning, mentorship and recognition that might otherwise be beyond their reach.

The impact of that approach was evident at last year’s competition, when two students from Pallebowala National School secured a remarkable victory with a project that impressed the judges through its creativity, problem-solving approach and potential impact, despite the students’ limited access to technology and facilities. Their achievement captured the spirit of Coolest Projects: innovation is not the preserve of those with the greatest resources, but can emerge wherever young people are given the opportunity to explore, experiment and create.

Coolest Projects provides an opportunity for young minds to go beyond consuming technology and begin creating solutions of their own. The Bank said it is particularly encouraged by the program’s reach beyond Colombo, recognising that talent and ingenuity exist in every part of the country and deserve the opportunity to flourish. Through its support, the Bank demonstrates its commitment to advancing digital literacy, education and youth empowerment through meaningful initiatives.

Coolest Projects is a globally recognised program delivered in countries including the United Kingdom, Ireland, Belgium, South Africa and Malaysia. Its international framework gives young Sri Lankan innovators an opportunity to present their work in an environment that celebrates creativity, technical achievement and practical problem-solving, while connecting their aspirations with a wider culture of technology-driven innovation. 

STEMUp Educational Foundation Co-Founder Prabhath Mannapperuma said: “Coolest Projects is about giving young people the space and encouragement to turn their curiosity into something tangible. An idea that begins as a simple experiment can develop into a meaningful technology project when students are challenged to think creatively, solve problems and learn from others. The mentoring journey is particularly important because it helps participants refine their ideas and strengthen their projects before presenting them to a wider audience. With the continued support of Commercial Bank, we are working to ensure that young innovators from across Sri Lanka have the opportunity to be seen, heard and encouraged to pursue their potential.”

Commercial Bank’s support for Coolest Projects Sri Lanka forms part of its broader ‘ComBank Akshara’ corporate social responsibility initiative, which seeks to advance STEM inclusion, digital literacy and youth empowerment. By supporting access to professional mentorship and opportunities for practical technology learning, the Bank aims to help bridge the digital divide and expand the horizons of students from both urban and rural communities.

The partnership also builds on a wider history of collaboration between Commercial Bank and the STEMUp Educational Foundation, including joint Day of Code initiatives conducted in 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025, and previous Coolest Projects showcases in Colombo in 2024 and 2025. Beyond financial support, the Bank is participating in the execution of the 2026 program, including event organisation, the evaluation process and support on the showcase day.

As the registration phase approaches its close, the spotlight now turns to the ideas that will emerge from classrooms, homes and communities across Sri Lanka. For the young people taking part, Coolest Projects offers more than a competition: it is an opportunity to test their ingenuity, learn from industry professionals and demonstrate how technology can turn a promising idea into a practical solution. In December, the country will discover which projects stand out, but the journey of discovery has already begun.

title: Indian High Commissioner backs SLUDI,  startups and AI at Digital Sri Lanka Summit 2026 | Daily FT

India is ready to move from sharing experiences to building digital capabilities with Sri Lanka, High Commissioner Santosh Jha said at the Digital Sri Lanka Summit 2026 on Thursday, pointing to around Rs. 25 billion in support for the national digital ID project (SLUDI), growing startup ties, disaster-tech cooperation after Cyclone Ditwah, and early work on Sinhala AI models.

Highlighting the scale and intensity of India’s digital transformation over the last decade, Jha spoke about India’s experience in developing population-scale Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), guided by the principles of inclusion, interoperability and openness. title: Temporary ETA waiver needs proof travellers can show at check-in | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 28 November 2026 00:00
-     - 29

By Douglas Vandergraph

When an official travel website goes down, the passenger at the airline counter becomes the final test of government communication. Sri Lanka’s temporary Electronic Travel Authorisation arrangement is a sensible response to an unavailable portal. It will protect visitors and businesses only if the instruction given to airlines reaches the person checking a passport at an overseas airport.

Daily FT reported on 25 November that the Immigration and Emigration Department had allowed travellers from most eligible countries to board without obtaining prior ETA approval while its online system undergoes maintenance. A circular dated 23 November directs airlines and ground handlers to accommodate covered passengers. Eligible travellers may receive an ETA or Visit Visa on arrival at Bandaranaike International Airport or another relevant port of entry. The report also noted a significant unresolved question: announcements did not clarify whether the existing free tourist ETA arrangement for citizens of 40 countries applies to authorisations issued on arrival during the interruption.

That uncertainty deserves a precise answer, but the challenge begins before arrival. A traveller may encounter an airline agent who has not seen the circular, a website still displaying old instructions or a booking system that insists on an authorisation number. The passenger cannot reasonably be expected to negotiate immigration policy at a departure gate. A public rule has little value if the people responsible for applying it see different versions.

The department could issue a dated, downloadable travel notice specifically for passengers and carriers. It should state the start of the temporary measure, the eligible nationalities or clear eligibility criteria, what documents must still be carried, where arrival permission is processed and which questions remain subject to normal immigration discretion. The notice should avoid promising that every traveller will be admitted merely because the advance ETA is waived. Eligibility to board and permission to enter are different decisions.

A separate one-page operational instruction for airline agents could use the same version number and provide a verified official route for checking unusual cases. Government authorities, aviation partners and Sri Lankan diplomatic missions could link to a single current notice instead of maintaining several slightly different copies. If the policy changes, an archived version and effective time would help settle disputes without leaving travellers to rely on a screenshot.

Fee clarity is part of the consumer problem. If free tourist ETAs normally apply to specified nationalities but temporary arrival processing is treated differently, the government should say so before travellers leave home. Any applicable fee, method of payment and official receipt process should be published. It is better to explain an unsettled point openly than to let private travel companies present conflicting guesses as official rules.

The system also needs a correction route. An eligible traveller turned away at check-in because an airline’s records are outdated should have a way to report the incident, including the flight, date and nature of the problem, without sharing passport images publicly. Airlines should be able to ask for urgent clarification through recognised operational channels. A useful complaint service is one that can fix the rule’s application, not merely apologise after a holiday has been lost.

Tourism operators have a role to play without becoming immigration advisers. Hotels and tour companies can direct guests to the authoritative notice, remind them that ordinary passport and entry requirements still apply and avoid charging for unofficial solutions. They should not be expected to guarantee an immigration outcome that only the competent authority can decide.

Once the portal returns, a brief service review could ask how long it was unavailable, how quickly the carrier instruction reached participating airlines, which traveller questions recurred and what was changed to prevent confusion next time. It need not expose security details about the system. Such a review would be especially useful for a country whose tourism and business travel depend on predictable entry procedures.

Jesus’ teaching about truthful speech is a reminder that a promise should be dependable in the ordinary situations where people act upon it. Here, good public service means more than announcing flexibility. It means ensuring the check-in desk has the same clear answer as the ministry.

Sri Lanka’s temporary waiver can spare visitors unnecessary disruption. The strongest next step is a current public notice that a passenger can show, a carrier can verify and the authorities can promptly correct. That is the difference between a good policy and a journey that actually works.

title: Attacks on humanitarian  assistance in Sri Lanka: 20  years on | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 28 November 2026 00:00
-     - 35

The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) has issued a Brief on attacks against humanitarian personnel, medical facilities and relief operations during Sri Lanka’s armed conflict. It finds that these attacks formed part of a sustained pattern, and that two decades later, accountability remains largely absent. Following is the Executive Summary of the Brief, titled ‘Attacks on Humanitarian Assistance in Sri Lanka, 20 Years On: I Died Many Times’.

Executive summary

Issued pursuant to the mandate of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights under General Assembly resolution 48/141 and Human Rights Council resolutions 46/1, 51/1, 57/1 and 60/1, this Brief documents the pattern of attacks against humanitarian personnel, medical and humanitarian infrastructure, and relief operations during Sri Lanka’s armed conflict, particularly between 2006 and May 2009.

Drawing on information and evidence compiled in OHCHR’s repository and consultations with 16 individuals engaged in humanitarian operations and medical service provision in conflict-affected areas between 2005 and 2009, the Brief finds that attacks on humanitarian actors and objects, restrictions on humanitarian access and the denial of essential assistance were neither isolated incidents nor incidental consequences of hostilities. Rather, they formed part of a sustained pattern that progressively dismantled humanitarian capacity, deepened civilian suffering and deprived affected populations of life-saving assistance and protection. 

This contributed to one of the most severe collapses of humanitarian protection recorded in a contemporary armed conflict. Two decades later, accountability for these serious violations of international law remains largely absent. This impunity continues to weigh on the families of those killed and injured and on their surviving colleagues, who remain without recognition or redress.

The Sri Lankan record acquires particular salience in the present moment. Attacks against humanitarian personnel, infrastructure and operations, alongside the denial or restriction of humanitarian access, have become defining features of contemporary armed conflicts. 

More than 1,010 humanitarian workers were killed between 2023 and 2025, almost three times the figure recorded in the preceding three years. The Inter-Agency Standing Committee has described the present period as an ‘era of impunity’. Many of those consulted for this Brief drew the parallel with other contemporary conflicts unprompted and in strikingly similar terms, describing the impunity that followed Sri Lanka’s war as a precedent that emboldened perpetrators elsewhere.

Contextual background

Restrictions on humanitarian access predated the final phase of the conflict and were imposed by all parties, albeit in different forms. Successive Governments restricted the movement of essential goods and humanitarian operations in areas controlled by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), while humanitarian organisations faced surveillance, arbitrary searches, checkpoint delays and restrictions on supplies. The LTTE also imposed restrictions on civilian movement and humanitarian personnel, including through its pass system. These measures progressively weakened humanitarian capacity and increased civilian vulnerability. United Nations assessments warned, even before 2006, that the humanitarian response was ill-equipped to withstand a major military offensive.

From 2006 onwards, these restrictions escalated into direct attacks on humanitarian personnel and infrastructure. Local organisations, particularly in Tamil-majority areas, also faced surveillance, asset freezes and proscription, while official narratives portraying humanitarian personnel as LTTE sympathisers further undermined their security. 

A decisive turning point came in September 2008, when the Government ordered United Nations agencies and international NGOs to withdraw from the Vanni. The subsequent departure of international personnel, followed by the withdrawal of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) from land-based operations in February 2009, severely reduced humanitarian access and removed a critical protection and monitoring presence.

During the final offensive, attacks on medical facilities escalated. Restrictions on food and medical supplies also intensified, with deliveries falling far below assessed requirements. Severe shortages of essential medicines and surgical equipment compromised medical treatment, while malnutrition and hunger reached critical levels. By the final weeks, civilians trapped in a narrow coastal strip under continuous shelling had virtually no access to humanitarian assistance, and the last functioning hospital had ceased operating.

The Brief examines four emblematic incidents: the disappearance of staff members of the Tamil Rehabilitation Organisation on 29 and 30 January, 2006; the killing of 17 Action Contre la Faim (ACF) staff in Muttur in August 2006; the shelling and obstruction of United Nations ‘Convoy 11’ in January 2009; and the shelling of Puthukkudiyiruppu (PTK) Hospital between January and February 2009. In none of them has any individual been held criminally responsible. 

The available evidence suggests that attacks, restrictions and deprivations affecting civilians and humanitarian relief occurred despite the Government’s knowledge of civilian locations and humanitarian needs. The Secretary-General’s Panel of Experts found credible allegations that Government forces had committed war crimes, including attacks on medical and humanitarian objects and the starvation of civilians through the denial of humanitarian relief, while the OHCHR Investigation on Sri Lanka (OISL) report found reasonable grounds to believe that numerous serious violations by all parties may amount to war crimes.

However, despite extensive documentation gathered over the years, meaningful accountability has yet to ensue, with the cases examined in this Brief exposing persistent drivers of impunity, including denial of State responsibility, ineffective investigations and prosecutions, inadequate protection of victims and witnesses, and reliance on commissions of inquiry in place of criminal accountability.

The Brief also examines the United Nations’ own response. It recalls the finding of the Secretary-General’s Internal Review Panel that, despite the courage shown by individual staff members, the United Nations failed to meet its responsibilities to protect civilians, respond to early warnings and ensure principled humanitarian and human rights action. These failures do not diminish the State’s primary responsibility to investigate and prosecute serious violations.

Voices of humanitarians

The consultations carried out revealed strikingly consistent accounts of the final phase of the conflict and its enduring consequences. Consultees described how humanitarian work itself became grounds for suspicion and intimidation, with national staff particularly exposed. They identified the withdrawal of international organisations in September 2008 as a decisive turning point that deprived civilians not only of humanitarian assistance but also of an international presence capable of witnessing and documenting violations.

Many described the progressive restriction and manipulation of humanitarian assistance as contributing to increasingly unbearable conditions for civilians trapped in the conflict area.

Medical personnel recalled working with overwhelming numbers of wounded and critically ill patients while lacking essential supplies, often unable to provide life-saving treatment. Humanitarian workers spoke of profound powerlessness, but also of a lasting sense of responsibility to bear witness to what they had experienced. For many, trauma and distress have persisted, compounded by years of unsuccessful efforts to obtain truth, recognition and accountability. The continued impunity leaves those affected without recognition, truth or redress, while reinforcing concerns that failure to address such violations risks their recurrence elsewhere.

Conclusion and recommendations

The report was shared with the Government of Sri Lanka in advance of its publication, providing an opportunity to comment, but no reply had been received by the time of publication.

OHCHR calls for a clear commitment to truth, accountability and non-recurrence, beginning with the State’s formal acknowledgement of attacks against humanitarian and medical personnel, facilities and operations, including those involving State security forces, and a public apology, together with adequate and comprehensive reparations for the families of those killed or disappeared and for surviving colleagues.

Prompt, independent and impartial investigations should address not only individual incidents but also whether attacks against humanitarian actors and restrictions on humanitarian assistance formed part of a broader policy or plan. This requires strengthening the independence and capacity of prosecutorial institutions, establishing an independent prosecutorial mechanism, incorporating war crimes and crimes against humanity into domestic legislation, and acceding to relevant international instruments, including the Rome Statute.

The Government should also take concrete measures to prevent recurrence by reforming the security sector, ensuring appropriate vetting of personnel implicated in serious violations, strengthening effective and independent victim and witness protection, and ending surveillance, intimidation and reprisals against victims, their families, human rights defenders and journalists.

OHCHR also recommends sustained international scrutiny and, where domestic efforts remain inadequate, support for accountability through international investigations, prosecutions, targeted sanctions and rigorous human rights vetting of Sri Lankan security personnel. 

Accountability for attacks against humanitarian action in Sri Lanka should form part of the broader international response to such violations, including efforts under Security Council resolution 2730 (2024) and the 2025 Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel, helping ensure that the impunity witnessed in Sri Lanka does not become a precedent for other conflicts.

title: A response to “Friends with all, subservient to none” | Daily FT
summary:

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake told Parliament on 20 March 2026 that under no circumstances, no matter the pressure, Sri Lanka would not undermine neutrality

The full title authored by Faiszer Mustapha, PC is “Friends with all, subservient to none: Why Sri Lanka must guard its national interests” (Daily FT, 24 November 2026, see: https://www.ft.lk/columns/Friends-with-all-subservient-to-none-Why-Sri-Lanka-must-guard-its-national-interest/4-800477).

The article states: “We must transparently and through established international procedures, so that no one says that Sri Lanka has taken sides in a war that is not ours. Parliament and the public deserve a clear account of the rules we are applying, who may enter our waters, on what terms, for how long, and what becomes of a vessel once it is in our custody. Neutrality is not silence, and it is not indifference. It is a principled position and must be explained clearly and consistently to all our partners East and West alike”.

This is exactly what the President of Sri Lanka did when he addressed Parliament on 20 March 2026 and stated: “Under no circumstances, no matter the pressure we encounter, will we permit this neutrality to be undermined,” he stressed.  

“With regard to the issue concerning Iranian vessels, a request was made to us on 26 February 2026 for three naval ships to visit Sri Lanka on 9 March and 13 as part of a goodwill visit aimed at strengthening cooperation. We were in the process of reviewing this request for approval. On the same evening, the United States also requested permission for two warfare aircraft to land at Mattala International Airport in Hambantota. He said that the Government took a firm decision based on the policy of maintaining neutrality and did not grant approval for either of these requests” (Daily News 21 March 2026).

Foundational principle of neutrality

“The sources of the international law of neutrality are customary international law and, for certain questions, international treaties, in particular the Paris Declaration of 1856, the 1907 Hague Convention No. V respecting the Rights and Duties of Neutral Powers and Persons in Case of War on Land, the 1907 Hague Convention No. XIII concerning the Rights and Duties of Neutral Powers in Naval War, the four 1949 Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocol I of 1977’ (ICRC, June 2022).

According to this publication the foundational principle is The Principle Of Inviolability of the Territory of the Neutral State. “The territory of a neutral State is inviolable. It is prohibited to commit any act of hostility whatsoever on such territory. Neutrality describes the formal position taken by a State which is not participating in an armed conflict or which does not want to become involved. This status entails specific rights and duties. On the one hand, the neutral State has the right to stand apart from and not be adversely affected by the conflict. On the other hand, it has a duty of non-participation and impartiality.

Furthermore, Neutral space comprises the national territory of the neutral State, its territorial waters and its national air space. Neutral persons are nationals of neutral states.

Although the article states that “Neutrality is not silence and it is not indifference,” it admits that it is “principled” without revealing their sources. However, the seriously flawed common notion is that Neutrality does not, by itself offer sufficient security. Such a perception is because they are unaware of the fact that it is Neutrality that offers security through the principle of Territorial inviolability. This foundational principle of Neutrality was recognised by both Iran and the USA when they accepted the response of the Sri Lankan Government to their requests.

Neutrality in the context of national interests            

The article refers to the “proposed $ 3.7 billion Sinopec oil refinery at Hambantota – described when it was signed in January 2025, as the largest foreign direct investment in our history.”  Had this project become a reality, there is a strong possibility that other major powers would have explored opportunities to set up mega projects in Trincomalee. Fortunately, for Sri Lanka negotiations are stalled. This has given Sri Lanka the opportunity to explore options that are in keeping with Sri Lanka’s needs and decided to expand the existing refinery at Sapugaskanda with a capacity of 100,000 Barrels per Day. The lesson to be learnt is that Sri Lanka should first decide on the scope and scale of projects to suit its national interests and then explore arrangements to finance them.

The approach adopted by Sri Lanka in this instance reflects not only mature and wise statecraft but also the opportunity to protect its strategic autonomy in keeping with its policy of Neutrality.   

Exercising domestic law

The article states: “The law is clear – those who come on tourist visas are not permitted to do business here. According to the  Sri Lankan Tourism Development Authority 75 foreign nationals were arrested and 15 deported last year for doing business while on tourist visas.” 

Judging from the experiences of Sri Lankans, the prevailing situation needs serious attention. In this regard, there is no question that the author with his distinguished knowledge and experience in 

politics and the law is most qualified to file a Writ of Mandamus in the Court of Appeal to ensure that all institutions associated with law enforcement relating to those operating businesses are qualified to do so with due diligence.

title: Sri Lanka opens doors to 1.4 b Chinese, but Sri Lankan traders still face a visa wall to China | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 28 November 2026 00:09
-     - 18

China’s Ambassador to Sri Lanka, Wei Huaxiang, has been active in Sri Lankan media and public diplomacy, emphasising China’s development opportunities and the prospects for bilateral cooperation. Beijing has consistently encouraged Sri Lankan businesses to use platforms such as the China International Import Expo and the Canton Fair to access the Chinese market. Yet if Sri Lankan traders cannot obtain a business visa within a reasonable and predictable timeframe, those trade promotion pledges ring hollow

By a Special Correspondent

As Sri Lanka rolls out the red carpet for Chinese travellers with free electronic travel authorisations (ETAs), a stark asymmetry is increasingly troubling the island’s business community: Sri Lankan citizens—particularly entrepreneurs who shuttle between Colombo and Guangzhou or Shanghai—continue to navigate a cumbersome, time-consuming and uncertain visa process for China.

This imbalance feels particularly jarring at a time when bilateral relations under the Belt and Road Initiative are supposedly at their warmest. Sri Lankan business circles are now urging the new Chinese Ambassador in Colombo to confront this bottleneck directly and recommend practical solutions to Beijing.

Sri Lanka’s open door for Chinese visitors

According to Sri Lanka’s Department of Immigration and Emigration, nationals of 40 countries—including China—are eligible for a free tourist ETA valid for 30 days, effective from May 2026. The scheme permits double entry within the validity period. The message to Chinese tourists and business travellers is unambiguous: Sri Lanka is open, and it is free.

The Chinese visa maze for Sri Lankans

The experience for a Sri Lankan travelling in the opposite direction is markedly different.

Since June 2025, the Chinese Embassy in Colombo has operated an online visa processing system. The official guidance is explicit about the timeline: after submitting an application online, applicants must wait 1 to 3 working days for preliminary review. Once approved, they must appear in person at the Embassy to submit their passport and biometric data. The visa processing itself then takes another 3 to 4 working days.

The Embassy does not accept postal applications. For a businessman based in Kandy or Galle, this means two separate trips to Colombo—one to submit documents, another to collect the passport—or the cost of engaging an agent.

In September 2025, the Embassy issued a notice acknowledging that applications had surged following the launch of the online system, and that some applicants had experienced longer processing times. The Embassy advised applicants to submit their materials 15 to 30 days in advance to avoid disrupting travel plans.

For a Sri Lankan entrepreneur with a long history of legitimate travel to China—someone who has attended the Canton Fair or the China International Import Expo multiple times—this process offers little recognition of that track record. Every trip begins anew with the same queue, the same waiting periods and the same uncertainty.

The Official Passport blind spot

A persistent observation in Colombo’s diplomatic and business circles is that Sri Lanka’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has not made Chinese visa facilitation a priority lobbying item. The reason, according to several business sources who spoke on condition of anonymity, is structural: senior officials and most Government leaders hold diplomatic or official passports.

Under the 2012 bilateral agreement, holders of diplomatic and official passports between China and Sri Lanka are exempt from visa requirements. Those who shape visa policy do not personally experience the queue, the fingerprinting or the fortnight-long wait that ordinary passport holders endure.

“The people who need to go to China to sell Ceylon tea, gemstones, or to seek manufacturing partnerships are precisely the private sector—the ones with ordinary passports,” one Colombo-based exporter told this correspondent. “We respect China’s sovereignty and security considerations. But when Chinese leaders speak of a ‘community with a shared future’ and the Belt and Road, facilitation of people-to-people flows should not be a one-way street.”

An opportunity for the New Ambassador

China’s Ambassador to Sri Lanka, Wei Huaxiang has been active in Sri Lankan media and public diplomacy, emphasising China’s development opportunities and the prospects for bilateral cooperation. Beijing has consistently encouraged Sri Lankan businesses to use platforms such as the China International Import Expo and the Canton Fair to access the Chinese market.

Yet if Sri Lankan traders cannot obtain a business visa within a reasonable and predictable timeframe, those trade promotion pledges ring hollow.

China has, in recent years, extended unilateral visa-free entry to ordinary passport holders from dozens of countries—including Japan, Australia, and several European nations—for business, tourism and transit purposes, for stays of up to 30 days. Sri Lanka, while not a wealthy nation, is a key node on the Maritime Silk Road and a long-standing partner. Analysts suggest several possible solutions: multi-year, multiple-entry visas for Sri Lankan business travellers with a clean travel history; a streamlined channel for those attending officially recognised trade fairs or business events; or a reciprocal business travel facilitation arrangement negotiated between the two governments.

The Chinese Embassy has stated its commitment to “facilitating visa applications for Sri Lankan friends travelling to China” and says it will “continue to introduce new measures to facilitate China-Sri Lanka personnel exchanges.” Business leaders say they would welcome concrete steps.

Way forward

Sri Lanka has extended its hand to Chinese visitors with a free ETA. That hand is open at the airport counter in Katunayake. But when a Sri Lankan trader reaches out to grasp it in return, they find their own hand bound by forms, two mandatory Embassy visits, and a wait that can stretch beyond two weeks.

For a new Ambassador who has already shown a willingness to engage publicly, resolving this “one-way facilitation” may be a more tangible demonstration of friendship than any grand narrative. After all, the Belt and Road is not only about port cranes and railway tracks. It is also about a small businessman in Colombo being able to fly to Guangzhou with reasonable ease—to sell a shipment of tea, or to buy a machine.

title: Why ethics must shape research training of degree students | Daily FT
summary:
