This article is based on an oration organised by the Sri Lanka Association for the Advancement of Science (SLAAS) in honour of the late Prof. S. R. Kottegoda, who laid the foundation for research ethics in Sri Lanka and made significant contributions to medical education, research and practice. Prof. Kottegoda established SLAAS’s ethics committee, the oldest in Sri Lanka. He was committed to ensuring that scientific research was carried out with integrity, accountability and respect for human values.

Introduction

Reviewing the history of research ethics is important for laying the foundation for this article. The earliest recorded cases involving research ethics relate directly to medicine and date from 1500 to 1700. The Nazi human experiments conducted on prisoners during the 1930s and 1940s are probably the first comprehensively investigated and well-documented major ethical violations in research. They led to the establishment of the Nuremberg Code (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg_Code), which required voluntary consent, risk minimisation, and scientific necessity. The Tuskegee Syphilis Study and the discovery of congenital disabilities in children due to an inadequately tested drug raised growing concerns about research ethics. A major international development in research ethics was the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki (https://www.wma.net/), which set out ethical principles for medical research involving human subjects. Another development was the Belmont Report (https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/belmont-report/index.html), which established the principles of respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. As a result, institutions conducting medical research established research ethics committees and boards to oversee research involving human subjects and ensure ethical standards.

Today, global research is a multi-trillion-dollar enterprise funded by governments and others, including individual donors, industry and business. We conduct research in a complex environment where competition for funding, conflicts of interest, research data, the training of highly qualified people, research dissemination, national and international rankings, and other factors affect research quality, integrity and outcomes. The importance of research ethics extends far beyond medicine and research involving human subjects. Therefore, this article addresses a topic at the very core of the research enterprise: research ethics and the training of research degree students.

At no point in history has this responsibility been more significant than it is now, as artificial intelligence reshapes research methods, conduct, and dissemination. Data can be collected, tampered with, analysed, and disseminated at unprecedented speed. Research collaborations increasingly transcend geographical, legal, and cultural boundaries, while political ideologies and differences have affected research through boycotts and restrictions on collaboration. Public trust in expertise is continually tested. 

Training research degree students (e.g., MPhil/PhD) is an important responsibility of the modern research enterprise. Students participate in grant proposal preparation, conduct research, create and manage data, and contribute to research dissemination. They are the future guardians of the research enterprise, and their training must include research ethics, integrity and responsible conduct. In this context, several issues at the core of the modern research enterprise require attention.  

Why must research ethics shape research training?

A key message here is that research ethics is no longer simply about compliance; it is essential to maintaining trust in scholarship. Assuming researchers are trustworthy, we are granted extraordinary privileges such as:

In return, society expects researchers to act responsibly. Important to recognise that research ethics emerged largely in response to historical ethical failures.

Training institutions must ensure that research degree students have more than disciplinary and methodological expertise. Students must be trained in moral judgement. The best approach for supervisors is not just to preach ethics but to practise it at every stage of research. Students readily follow their supervisors’ practices and judgements. Research advisors must educate students about these responsibilities, and students should constantly reflect on them when they engage in research. Therefore, supervisors must always emphasise that ethics protects participants, researchers, institutions and public confidence.

Prof. S.R. Kottegoda

Around the world, examples show that ethical failures rarely arise from ignorance alone. They often emerge from poor research cultures. Unfortunately, these cultures grow because of the competitiveness of the research enterprise.

International best practices in research ethics and integrity education

As institutions develop integrity-based research cultures, five international best practices have emerged.

a) Ethics across the entire research lifecycle – Requires ethics to be embedded throughout proposal development, data collection, experimentation, analysis, publication and dissemination. Ethics does not end once the ethics committee approves the proposal. In fact, it really starts after the committee’s approval.

b) Mandatory integrity training - Many institutions today require ethics certification, integrity modules and refresher courses before students commence independent research.  

c) Supervisor training - An important aspect of research student training is the relationship between supervisors and students. Supervisory behaviour strongly influences student practices. Students often adopt the ethical standards their supervisors demonstrate. 

d) Open science and data stewardship - With the increasing focus on transparent research and open access to research data, scholarly journals and granting agencies now require researchers to provide access to the data and methods used in their research. Today, credible research journals require authors to include a statement on data access and sufficient details about methods and tools. 

e) Community and indigenous engagement - Research increasingly involves community and Indigenous engagement and emphasises the importance of respecting traditions, values and cultures when conducting research. Under these conditions, modern ethical frameworks require recognising participants as partners rather than subjects. This represents a significant shift in ethical thinking. 

Readers interested in best practices may review the following sites and documents: UK Research Integrity Office, Canadian Tri-Council Responsible Conduct of Research Framework, Australian Code for the Responsible Conduct of Research, Singapore Statement on Research Integrity and European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity. 

Canadian Tri-Council Policy Statement (TCPS 2)

Canada’s Tri-Council Policy Statement: Ethical Conduct for Research Involving Humans (TCPS 2) is among the world’s most comprehensive research ethics frameworks (https://ethics.gc.ca/eng/policy-politique_tcps2-eptc2_2022.html). It is jointly administered by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.

Its importance lies in its emphasis on principles rather than rules. Three core principles underpin TCPS 2. They are: Respect for Persons, Concern for Welfare and Justice. Respect for Persons recognises human dignity, autonomy, and informed consent; Concern for Welfare must consider physical, psychological, economic, and social wellbeing; and Justice must ensure fair participant selection, inclusion, and equity. These three principles form the ethical foundation for research involving humans. TCPS 2 provides flexibility, allows ethical judgment rather than rigid compliance, encourages inclusivity, and applies across disciplines. TCPS also emphasises risk-based reviews, requiring more intensive scrutiny for higher-risk research.

An important element of the TCPS is its dedicated approach to research involving Indigenous communities. The framework emphasises respect, reciprocity, partnership and community engagement. A key element of TCPS 2 is moving from protecting participants to respecting them.

Responsible Conduct of Research Framework (RCRF)

The modern research enterprise requires us to recognise that research ethics and integrity extend far beyond protection for human participants. The Canadian Tri-Agency Framework: Responsible Conduct of Research (https://rcr.ethics.gc.ca/eng/home.html) establishes responsibilities for researchers, institutions and funding agencies. The objective of RCRF is to strengthen research integrity throughout the research ecosystem. Key expectations include honesty, presenting findings truthfully, rigour, using appropriate methods, transparency, maintaining complete records, accountability, accepting responsibility for decisions, stewardship, and responsible management of funding. The framework also identifies misconduct such as fabrication, falsification, plagiarism, inappropriate authorship, misrepresentation and mismanagement of research funds.

Training research degree students

For research degrees, there are high entry requirements, prestigious scholarships, rigorous assessments of research progress and publication requirements. Yet, most research degree students earn their degrees without understanding research ethics and integrity. Universities increasingly recognise the importance of research ethics and integrity, regardless of the research topic. Research degree programs must follow mandatory ethics and integrity training for all research degree students. International best practices require every doctoral and master’s student to complete structured training on ethics and the Responsible Conduct of Research. Supervisors have a moral responsibility to ensure that students understand publication ethics (acknowledgement of literature, plagiarism, proper authorship), data management (data records, data falsification, data ownership, etc.), AI governance (writing, analysis, funding agency and publication guidelines), authorship (no bogus authors, authorship reflects contributions), and conflict of interest (personal conflicts, favouritism, funding, etc.).

Supervisor development is an important element of institutional responsibility. Supervision of research degree students should be limited to those who have completed formal research ethics preparation. Many universities and granting agencies have prepared literature and developed tools to support research ethics training for supervisors. 

Universities should foster an ethical research culture by promoting and rewarding integrity, mentorship and responsible scholarship, rather than focusing solely on funding amounts and the number of papers published during performance reviews. For professorial promotions, emphasis should be placed on publication quality, the rigour of journals’ peer-review processes, the accomplishments of former research students, and peer recognitions, rather than turning promotion evaluation into a bean-counting exercise.

Reflective practices require students to be encouraged to discuss regularly the ethical dilemmas that arise during their candidature. Developing ethics through reflection, rather than regulation alone, is best practice. As researchers, we must always be self-critical, examining the quality and value of our work and constantly aspiring to meet high standards. The research degree students we train today are the future custodians of scholarship. Therefore, they must be trained not only to conduct research and publish papers but also to be ethical scholars worthy of public trust. 

Therefore, universities have a responsibility to cultivate researchers who can not only discover new knowledge but also be trusted to create it. 

AI and research ethics

AI will profoundly affect research and research integrity. AI presents both opportunities and challenges for research. It will provide new research opportunities and enhance scientific discovery. We must carefully address its ethical use in research and develop recommendations and guidelines to ensure it does not open the door to research misconduct and unethical practices. Funding agencies and universities have already begun addressing this important issue, and guidelines and recommendations are either in place or under development. In a recent article, David B. Resnik and Mohammad Hosseini, Northwestern University, USA, AI and Ethics (2025) 5:1499–1521, present nine recommendations covering ethical use of AI in research.

 Conclusion

Researchers are privileged individuals, and the public, governments, and business and industry support, celebrate and respect them. Over the past decades, funding for scientific research has increased, more advanced research infrastructure has been built, and a large global pool of talent has become available. So, while research resources are growing, there is also a growing trend of declining trust and ethical lapses.

Sri Lankan universities, research institutes, and funding agencies must establish frameworks on research ethics and integrity, develop guidelines on the responsible conduct of research, offer mandatory research ethics and integrity training for grantees, research supervisors, and graduate students, and develop mechanisms to investigate research misconduct.

(The author served at Canadian universities for over 35 years and held academic administrative roles as department head, dean, and vice-president for research and international. He is currently the Senior Deputy Vice-Chancellor And Provost of the Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology. He delivered the S.R. Kottegoda Oration at SLAAS’s invitation in October 2026)

title: Protecting the State or protecting its citizens? | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 28 November 2026 00:00
-     - 18

To foster sustainable economic development, national security, democratic accountability, and investor confidence should not be viewed as competing interests; they are essential pillars for building a prosperous future.

Sri Lanka finds itself at a crucial juncture in its journey towards economic stability and democratic resilience. After enduring a severe economic crisis, sovereign debt default, political turbulence, and a period of public uncertainty, the country now focuses on restoring international trust, attracting foreign direct investment (FDI), generating employment opportunities, and securing a viable economic future for younger generations.

In light of this context, the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTA), aimed at replacing the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA), as well as the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill (POCB), must be examined with due diligence.

The primary inquiry here is not whether Sri Lanka requires effective legislation to address terrorism and organised crime—clearly, it does. A responsible Government has an obligation to safeguard national security, maintain public order, and ensure the safety of its citizens. The more pressing concern, however, lies in determining whether this responsibility should be managed through legislation that may inadvertently consolidate significant power within the Executive, potentially impacting individual liberties, judicial independence, and democratic accountability.

For a developing economy seeking to attract international investment, this matter transcends mere constitutional debate; it encompasses critical economic considerations as well. 

Supreme Court’s Determination: Constitutional permission is not public endorsement

The Supreme Court has concluded that the PSTA may advance through Parliament with a simple majority, contingent upon four amendments at the Committee Stage, including:

1. Needing police applications for extended custody. 

2. Enhancing judicial oversight through the Supreme Court.

3. Omitting unnecessary provisions. 

4. Clarifying the judicial review process for executive orders.

The Court further indicated that the Bill should not simply be viewed as a continuation of the PTA, emphasising that legislation should be evaluated based on its actual safeguards rather than potential abuses by public officials.

While this determination warrants respect, it is vital to contextualise it within the broader constitutional framework. A judicial ruling on constitutional validity does not inherently validate that legislation aligns with sound public policy, meets international human rights standards, or possesses democratic legitimacy.

Sri Lanka’s constitutional history offers pertinent lessons. The 18th Amendment, while receiving judicial approval, was later met with criticism for centralising presidential power and eroding institutional checks and balances. Its principal components were subsequently reversed by the 19th Amendment, which then led to the reinstatement of significant executive powers through the 20th Amendment, and further curtailments in the 21st Amendment.

These experiences clearly demonstrate that constitutional permissibility and effective governance are not synonymous.

The responsibility for enacting sound legislation ultimately lies with Parliament, which must weigh not only what the Constitution permits but also what is necessary for the nation, its citizens, and its democratic institutions.

Concerns raised by the legal profession

The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL), led by President Rajeev Amarasuriya, has expressed serious reservations about both proposed Bills. These objections are not rooted in a general opposition to national security legislation but rather focus on the extent of executive authority, the potential weakening of judicial oversight, and the potential implications for fundamental freedoms.

The BASL has noted that the gazetted PSTA varies significantly from the earlier consultative draft, specifically regarding aspects of detention, bail, and judicial supervision. They have called for a re-evaluation of the Bill in its current form, publication of the committee report and dissenting views, and a thorough explanation from the Government regarding the changes introduced.

Concerns regarding the POCB are equally profound, particularly regarding its treatment of offenses connected to organised criminal groups, which may broaden criminal liability markedly. Criticism has also been levelled at the admissibility of certain confessions obtained by senior police officers and the constraints placed on judicial discretion concerning bail and remand.

The Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka has independently recommended that the POCB be withdrawn and substantially revised, highlighting concerns about its compatibility with constitutional protections and international human rights obligations.

These concerns reflect significant institutional objections that deserve thoughtful consideration and reasoned responses rather than political dismissal. 

Importance of international perspectives

The international community’s input is equally pertinent.

United Nations human rights experts, in a statement from November 9, 2026, commended the Government’s intention to repeal the PTA and acknowledged that the latest PSTA draft represents a notable improvement over previous versions. Nonetheless, they underscored the need for additional safeguards, including effective judicial oversight over detention, robust protections against torture, safeguarding journalists’ rights and their sources, as well as ensuring accountability for officials who violate the law.

Organisations such as Amnesty International have also raised concerns regarding the extensive nature of counterterrorism powers and their potential effects on freedoms of expression, association, and peaceful dissent.

Additionally, the European Union’s GSP+ framework is a crucial consideration, as Sri Lanka’s preferential access to this market is contingent upon upholding international conventions, including commitments related to human rights. Noncompliance with these obligations could have repercussions extending far beyond the legal and political realms.

Thus, the Government should view international scrutiny not as an infringement on national sovereignty but as an opportunity to strengthen it. Observance of voluntarily undertaken international obligations is a hallmark of responsible governance.

Economic significance: Investor confidence as cornerstone

One of the most critical yet often overlooked dimensions of this discourse is its economic significance.

Sri Lanka urgently requires sustainable FDI to enhance its productive capabilities, diversify its exports, facilitate technology transfer, generate employment opportunities, and improve foreign exchange earnings.

The Board of Investment has reported that FDI inflows reached approximately $ 1057 billion in 2025, signifying a 72% increase from the previous year. While this trend is encouraging, it should not obscure the substantial gap that remains between current investment levels and the ambitious development objectives of the country.

Foreign investors weigh their decisions on multiple factors beyond tax incentives, labor costs, geographical advantages, or political assurances. They seek predictability in legislation, consistency in taxation, transparency in procurement processes, reliable enforcement of contracts, independence of regulatory institutions, and access to effective legal remedies.

The U.S. Department of State and the U.S. International Trade Administration have identified challenges facing Sri Lanka, including regulatory unpredictability, bureaucratic inefficiencies, inconsistent policy implementation, and uncertainty surrounding investment approvals.

These challenges are particularly significant for investments in renewable energy, infrastructure, manufacturing, tourism, logistics, and technology, where substantial capital commitments are often made over extended periods.

A potential investor contemplating a long-term commitment requires assurance that commercial disputes will be resolved impartially, that regulations will not shift arbitrarily, and that public authorities will exercise their powers within clear legal frameworks. The rule of law is not merely an abstract concept; it represents an essential economic asset. 

Indeed, the principles that protect citizens from arbitrary detention simultaneously safeguard business owners from arbitrary administrative actions. Institutional accountability ultimately benefits all stakeholders.

Principle of separation of powers: Key safeguard

The principle of separation of powers, articulated by Montesquieu in his 1748 work The Spirit of the Laws, underscores a fundamental tenet: liberty is jeopardised when legislative, executive, and judicial powers are concentrated in a single entity.

The legislature creates laws, the executive enforces them, and the judiciary independently interprets and applies them. Each of these branches must operate within its constitutional boundaries while maintaining checks and balances to prevent arbitrary governance.

This is especially pertinent in the context of national security legislation, which inherently grants the State considerable authority over individual liberties. Consequently, independent judicial supervision is paramount.

Though a Government may hold a democratic mandate with a substantial parliamentary majority, that authority does not translate into unchecked power to diminish constitutional safeguards. Democracy encompasses not only majority rule but also protection for minority rights, respect for dissent, institutional independence, and equal treatment under the law.

Learning from Sri Lanka’s past

Sri Lanka has faced considerable challenges due to the previous misuse of extraordinary State powers. The PTA, initially introduced in 1979 as temporary legislation, became entrenched in the legal framework for decades. Its legacy illustrates how powers enacted under the guise of national security can extend beyond their original intent.

This ongoing discourse around the proposed Bills is rooted in real concerns, not theoretical apprehensions. Legal commentator Kishali Pinto Jayawardene highlights significant issues regarding the management of confidential information and the protection of whistleblowers. She argues that broadly defined national security restrictions may deter journalists, public-interest investigators, and whistleblowers from carrying out their vital roles in serving the public interest.

This consideration warrants serious attention. Accountability hinges on the capacity to question public authorities, expose misconduct, and scrutinise decisions made in the name of national security.

A nation cannot cultivate a credible investment environment while simultaneously fostering uncertainty around the legitimate exercise of freedom of expression and the right to access information. 

Recommendations for Government action

The Government should approach calls for re-evaluation not as a challenge to its development objectives or to national security but as an opportunity to embrace a more sophisticated and inclusive governance approach.

First, the PSTA and POCB should undergo thorough consultations with the BASL, the Human Rights Commission, civil society, independent legal experts, and relevant international bodies.

Second, the Government should articulate the rationale behind deviations from earlier consultative drafts and clarify how the proposed provisions satisfy both constitutional and international human rights standards.

Third, powers related to detention, bail restrictions, surveillance, and investigative procedures should be paired with effective judicial oversight, independent reviews, and accessible remedies to prevent abuse.

Fourth, the legislation should ensure sufficient protections for journalists, whistleblowers, lawyers, researchers, and individuals engaged in lawful civic activities.

Lastly, any organised crime legislation must be carefully crafted to distinguish genuine criminal organisations from legitimate trade unions, professional associations, peaceful demonstrations, and ordinary collective activities.

There exists no inherent conflict in maintaining robust national security legislation while also respecting these essential safeguards.

Message to next generation

For Sri Lanka’s young entrepreneurs, professionals, lawyers, academics, and future leaders, this dialogue holds significant relevance. They are the generation tasked with establishing businesses, attracting investments, generating employment, advancing technology, and rejuvenating a competitive economy.

They require a nation that enables the free expression of ideas, where commercial agreements are honoured, where public institutions are held accountable, and where the law is applied fairly to all.

A thriving economy cannot flourish amid uncertainty, just as a democratic society cannot thrive in an atmosphere of fear.

The Government has a unique opportunity to demonstrate that its commitment to economic recovery is paralleled by a strong dedication to democratic principles.

Investors seek not only a favourable investment climate but also a country characterised by predictability, credibility, and accountability in governance.

Moreover, it is crucial to remember that national security exists to protect the citizens of the State, not to make them vulnerable to the State’s authority. 

Ultimately, the true measure of a nation’s strength lies not in the extent of its Government’s power over its people but in how judiciously that power is wielded within the confines of the law.

Sri Lanka deserves security, investment, economic development, and political stability, but these cannot be sustained at the expense of liberty, justice, and public trust.

The Government should listen to the concerns raised by the legal community, independent institutions, international partners, and, most importantly, its citizens. Withdrawing and thoughtfully redrafting these Bills would not signify a retreat from governance; rather, it would showcase the maturity and confidence expected from a Government entrusted with the responsibility of nation-building.

The real test of leadership lies not merely in the ability to pass legislation with a parliamentary majority but in the capacity to enact laws that inspire trust and confidence among the populace.

title: Knee surgery rules Sinner out of Australian Open | Daily FT

Jannik Sinner has been ruled out of the Australian Open in January following an operation on his knee. The 25-year-old Italian, who won the 2024 and 2025 titles at Melbourne Park, has not played competitively since winning Wimbledon on 12 July.

In a social media post on Tuesday, world number two Sinner said he had undergone surgery to “improve the condition of my iliotibial band” - a thick band of tissue that runs along the outside of the knee.

“We’ve been in regular touch with Jannik’s team and they’ve confirmed he won’t be joining us for the AO (Australian Open) in January following his recent surgery,” said Tennis Australia chief executive Andrew Abdo.

“Jannik loves competing here in Melbourne and is looking forward to returning for AO 2028. We wish him all the very best with his recovery and look forward to seeing him back on court soon.” The 2027 Australian Open main draw starts on 17 January.

Sinner’s challenge at the 2026 tournament was ended by a five-set semi-final defeat by Novak Djokovic.

 Sinner was the dominant player for the first half of the season, winning 44 and losing just three of his singles matches.

He won five Masters 1000 titles in a row between March and May, becoming the youngest man to complete the ‘career Golden Masters’, and reclaimed the world’s top ranking from Alcaraz along the way. However, he suffered a shock second-round exit at the French Open, with Zverev ultimately stepping up to win his first Grand Slam title.

Sinner bounced back on the grass courts, demolishing Novak Djokovic in the semi-finals before coming back from a set down against Zverev in the Wimbledon showpiece. He ended his season in early October, meaning he was unable to defend the points he claimed with title triumphs in China, Vienna, Paris and the ATP Finals at the end of 2025.

Zverev went on to win the US Open and secure the year-end number one ranking.

FIFA has been hit by a criminal cyberattack in which hackers gained access to personal and business information.

The hack accounted for less than 0.1% of data held by FIFA and the documents taken did not include anything related to the controversial and ultimately doomed FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal.

The breach was not a result of systems or technology failure on FIFA’s part, adding that hackers gained access by impersonating staff.

A FIFA spokesperson said: “FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information. FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement.

“FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data. Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.”

A group called Handsome Boy Hacking Club appeared to claim responsibility for the attack after publishing screenshots of what appeared to be a FIFA computer desktop on its X account.

Jamie Overton

Jamie Overton took a career-best 5-12 as England thrashed Australia by seven wickets in the third T20 international in Brisbane on Friday.

Overton’s figures were the best by an Englishman against Australia in T20s as the home side were bundled out for 108, their lowest score on Australian soil.

 “I thought Jamie Overton was outstanding tonight,” England captain Harry Brook said. “He’s worked hard and put in some extra graft at training. He simplified his game and reaped the rewards tonight – he had it on a string and it felt like we could change the field and make them make a mistake.”

Brook won the toss and sent Australia in to bat, and off-spinner Liam Dawson struck early when he had Australian skipper Mitch Marsh caught at mid-on. Jake Fraser-McGurk and Sam Harper attacked during the powerplay, taking the score to 55 after five overs.

Harper raced to 26 off 14 balls before Dawson grabbed his second when the Australian wicketkeeper got a top edge to Overton at mid-on.

Overton then swung into action with the ball, claiming the next five wickets as Australia slumped from 65-2 to 92-7 and then collapsed to 108 all out when Sam Curran clean-bowled Billy Stanlake. Aneurin Donald, who smashed 85 off 32 on the Gold Coast on Tuesday, got the run chase off to a spectacular start, belting 31 from just 11 balls.

But a rain delay seemed to help the Australians, as Brook holed out for nine after play resumed, before Donald fell for 32, leaving England 49-3. Another rain break threatened to stop England’s momentum again, but Jordan Cox blasted 33 in quick time to give the visitors an easy win and go ahead in the five-game series 2-1.

The hero of the run chase Sineth Jayawardene obliges fans with a selfie

Player of the Match in Sri Lanka ‘A’s clinical run chase against India ‘A’, Sineth Jayawardena said that he was under a bit of pressure going into the match as he had not scored in the previous three games, but the conversation he had with his head coach Ashan Priyanjan helped him to put his mentality.

“My coaches helped me, and they said that I should trust my game. I went out with a positive mindset,” said Jayawardena whose fabulous knock of 105 off 70 balls set the platform for Sri Lanka ‘A’ to successfully chase down a target of 318 and win by eight wickets.

Sri Lanka ‘A’s authoritative win disappointed a lot of Indian cricket fans, not to mention the stakeholders who were looking forward to an India-Pakistan final.

Jayawardene said that nothing special was said to him nor his opening partner Lasith Croospulle when they began the run chase.   

“They told me and Croospulle to bat the way we normally bat and to do our basics. It was a really good wicket to bat on even when the Indians were batting.”

Jayawardene said that he was extremely happy to get a hundred especially with the support of the Sri Lankan spectators who were present and to win a match against India chasing a target of 318 and getting them in 42 overs was something he could not describe in words.

“In the first three matches I couldn’t get much runs but Croospulle told me the day I score runs the match is ours, so to curtail my stroke play. I got valuable advice from the other coaches and players as well. It gave me a lot of confidence to go out there and perform.”

The 21-year-old left-hander reached 50 off 35 balls and 100 off 62, and finished with 105 off 70, with 10 fours and 6 sixes. He put on 174 for the first wicket with Croospulle who also made a century. By the time Jayawardene was out the chase was all but done.

“I have a positive intent. If the ball is in my arc I will go after it,” said Jayawardene. “For me and the team we are planning to win the Asia Cup. We came to this tournament and took one match at a time. We never thought about qualifying for the final from the outset. That mindset has worked in favour of us. Whoever comes to the final we have to do our preparations well, play a good game of cricket and win the trophy”.

Sri Lanka will meet the winner of the second semi-final between Pakistan ‘A’ and Bangladesh ‘A’ in the final on Sunday.

Jayawardene looks a complete player, blessed with a natural ability to strike the ball cleanly and with an impressive range of shots. There is something exciting about the way he bats. Talent alone will not take him there. He needs to stay grounded, keep learning, do the hard yards and be prepared to overcome the challenges that will inevitably come his way. There is exciting talent surfacing but it needs to be managed properly if Sri Lanka is to build a team for the future. (ST)
